title: Hegra: A City Carved in Rock
summary: How the Nabataeans carved more than one hundred tombs into the sandstone of Hegra, near AlUla, and how trade helped the city grow, fade, and become Saudi Arabia's first World Heritage Site.
poll: Old places like Hegra are worth protecting for the future.

versions.title: A Town in the Rocks
versions.text:
Go far north in Saudi Arabia. See the tall red hills. Near them is an old town. It is Hegra.

The town is two thousand years old. The Nabataeans built it. They built Petra, too.

The rock here is sandstone. It is soft. It is easy to cut. Men chose to carve tombs here. A tomb holds the dead. There are more than one hundred! Some have birds on them.

One tomb stands on its own. It is one big rock. The bottom is not done. The men cut from the top down.

Words are cut over the doors. They name who owns it. In time, this script grew. It led to the one for Arabic.

The town was a stop for trade. Long lines of camels came. Each was a caravan. They took goods that smell sweet. It had lots of wells. Men and beasts drank there.

The homes were made of mud. Most are gone. The tombs are still here. In 2008, it made a world list of great sites. It was the first in Saudi Arabia.

In the north of Saudi Arabia, there are tall hills of red and gold rock. Near them is a very old town called Hegra.

Hegra was built about two thousand years ago. The people who built it were called the Nabataeans. They also built the famous town of Petra in Jordan.

The rock here is sandstone. It is soft, so it is easy to cut. The workers chose to carve huge tombs right into the hills. A tomb is a place where the dead are buried. There are more than one hundred tombs! Some have birds and step shapes cut on the front.

One big tomb stands all alone. It was cut from one huge rock. Its bottom part was never finished. This shows that the workers cut from the top down.

Words are carved above many doors. They tell who owns each tomb. The script they used later grew into the script we use for Arabic.

Hegra was a key stop for trade. Long lines of camels, called caravans, passed through. The camels carried goods that smelled sweet. The town had many wells, so people and camels could drink.

The homes were made of mud, and most of them are gone now. But the tombs are still here. In 2008, Hegra was put on a world list of great sites. It was the first place in Saudi Arabia on that list.

One large tomb stands all alone. It was cut from a single giant rock. Its bottom part was never finished. This shows that the workers carved from the top down.

Words are carved above many of the doors. They tell who owned each tomb. The script they used later grew into the script we use for Arabic.

Hegra was a key stop for trade. Long lines of camels, called caravans, passed through the town. They carried sweet-smelling goods. Hegra had many wells, so people and camels could drink.

The homes in Hegra were made of mud, and most are gone now. But the tombs still stand. In 2008, Hegra was put on a world list of great sites. It was the first place in Saudi Arabia on that list.

versions.title: Hegra: A City Carved in Rock
versions.text:
In the northwest of Saudi Arabia lies AlUla, a valley of giant rocks in shades of red and gold. Near AlUla is an ancient city called Hegra, also known as Al-Hijr. It is one of the most special places in the country.

Hegra was built about two thousand years ago by the Nabataeans. They are the same people who built the famous city of Petra in Jordan. Hegra was their most important city in the south of their kingdom.

The rock here is sandstone, which is soft enough to cut. Using simple tools, Nabataean workers carved more than one hundred huge tombs into the sides of the rocky hills. A tomb is a place where people are buried. Each tomb is a monument with a decorated front. Many have step shapes at the top, and some have carved eagles above the door.

The most famous tomb stands all by itself. It was carved from a single giant rock. Its bottom part was never finished. This tells us that the workers carved from the top down.

Above many doors is an inscription, or carved writing. It tells who owned the tomb. The Nabataeans wrote in a script that later developed into the Arabic script.

Hegra was an important stop on a trade road. Caravans of camels carried incense from southern Arabia to lands in the north. Incense is sweet-smelling tree sap that people burned. Hegra had many wells, so travelers could rest and drink.

The homes in Hegra were made of mud bricks, and most have crumbled away. The stone tombs, however, are still standing. In 2008, Hegra became the first place in Saudi Arabia on the World Heritage List.

versions.title: Hegra: A City Carved in Rock
versions.text:
In the northwest of Saudi Arabia lies AlUla, a valley of towering rock formations in shades of red and gold, and near it stands an ancient city called Hegra, also known as Al-Hijr. Today it is one of the most remarkable historical sites in the country, and archaeologists from Saudi Arabia and other nations continue to study it.

Hegra was established approximately two thousand years ago by the Nabataeans, the same civilization that built the famous city of Petra in Jordan. Hegra was their most significant settlement in the southern part of their kingdom.

The rock here is sandstone, which is soft enough to cut with simple tools. Nabataean workers carved more than one hundred enormous tombs into the sides of the rocky outcrops, and each tomb has a decorated facade, or front, that resembles the entrance of a grand building. Many display step-shaped designs at the top, and some feature carved eagles above the entrance.

The most famous tomb stands completely isolated. It was carved from a single massive rock, but its lower section was never finished, which reveals that the workers carved from the top down.

Above many entrances is an inscription that identifies who owned the tomb, and some inscriptions even warn that anyone who misuses the tomb must pay a fine. The Nabataeans wrote in a script that eventually developed into the Arabic script.

Hegra was able to prosper because it was a stop on a trade route. Caravans of camels transported incense, a fragrant tree resin that people burned, from southern Arabia to territories in the north, and the city's numerous wells allowed travelers to rest and drink.

Hegra's success did not last forever. In the year 106, the Roman Empire took control of the Nabataean kingdom, and over the following centuries merchants shipped more of their goods by sea along the Red Sea coast. As fewer caravans crossed the desert, the city slowly declined.

The residences in Hegra were constructed from mud bricks, and most have crumbled away, while the stone tombs have survived. In 2008, Hegra became the first location in Saudi Arabia on the World Heritage List, which recognizes places that are important to all of humanity.

versions.title: Hegra: A City Carved in Rock
versions.text:
In the northwest of Saudi Arabia lies AlUla, a valley of towering rock formations in shades of crimson and gold, and near it stands an ancient city called Hegra, also known as Al-Hijr. Today it is among the most extraordinary historical sites in the kingdom, and archaeologists from Saudi Arabia and other nations continue to investigate its secrets.

Hegra was established approximately two thousand years ago by the Nabataeans, the same civilization that constructed the celebrated city of Petra in Jordan, and it functioned as their most significant settlement in the southern portion of their kingdom.

The local rock is sandstone, which is sufficiently soft to cut with relatively simple tools. Nabataean craftsmen carved more than one hundred enormous tombs into the sides of the rocky outcrops, and each tomb possesses an elaborately decorated facade, or front, that resembles the entrance of a monumental building. Many display step-shaped designs at the summit, and several feature carved eagles above the entrance.

The most celebrated tomb stands completely isolated, carved from a single massive boulder, but its lower section was never completed, which demonstrates that the craftsmen carved systematically from the top downward.

Above numerous entrances is an inscription that identifies the tomb's owner, and some inscriptions even warn that anyone who misuses the tomb must pay a substantial fine. The Nabataeans wrote in a distinctive script that eventually evolved into the Arabic script.

Hegra was able to prosper because it served as a stop on an important commercial route. Caravans of camels transported incense, a fragrant tree resin that people burned, from southern Arabia to territories in the north, and the city's numerous wells allowed exhausted travelers to rest and replenish their supplies.

Hegra's prosperity, however, did not endure indefinitely, since in the year 106 the Roman Empire annexed the Nabataean kingdom, and over the following centuries merchants increasingly transported their goods by sea along the Red Sea coast, so progressively fewer caravans needed to traverse the desert and the city gradually declined.

The residences in Hegra were constructed from perishable mud bricks, and most have consequently crumbled away, whereas the stone tombs have endured for centuries. In 2008, Hegra became the first location in Saudi Arabia to be inscribed on the World Heritage List, which recognizes places of exceptional importance to all of humanity.

HIGH.prompt: Some people say Hegra's tombs teach us more about the Nabataeans than any book could. Do you agree or disagree? Support your position with evidence from the article.
checklist: I supported it with at least two pieces of evidence from the article.
I explained how my evidence supports my position.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I agree that Hegra's tombs teach us more about the Nabataeans than any book could, because the carved facades are physical evidence that no written record can fully replace. Each tomb's inscription names its owner, giving archaeologists exact proof of who lived in this kingdom and prospered there two thousand years ago. The unfinished tomb, carved from a single rock from the top down, even reveals the Nabataeans' building methods, a detail a simple written history would rarely describe so precisely. For these reasons, the tombs offer a direct, lasting heritage that goes beyond anything a book alone could tell us.
